..
As of 200 PM Thursday... 

KEY MESSAGE 1... A pair of cold fronts will bring gusty winds and 
potentially a few light showers this afternoon and tomorrow. A 
Freeze Watch has been issued for our northern counties Friday night 
to early Saturday.

Satellite imagery along with surface observations indicate that the 
cold front has passed the Triad and nearing the Triangle. The front 
is expected to move through all of central NC by late this afternoon 
to early evening. Along and behind the front, gusts out of the WNW 
will range from 25-30 mph, before diminishing this evening and 
tonight. Temperatures will fall this evening post-frontal, but stay 
above freezing in the upper 30s to middle 40s.

This afternoon ahead of the front, the HRRR/RRFS are indicating a 
small sliver of instability, mainly near/along and east of the US-1 
corridor. A few sprinkles or showers will accompany the front for 
portions of the Triangle, Sandhills, and Coastal Plain late this 
afternoon, but most areas will see no more than a trace of rainfall.

A secondary cold front will move through Friday night, with the 
airmass significantly turning colder to values typical for late 
December or early January. A secondary shortwave rotating around the 
base of the trough will bring some late day clouds and perhaps a few 
isolated sprinkles or light rain, mainly for the Triangle north and 
east. Again, this is going to be very light at best, with most areas 
only seeing a trace to at most a few hundredths of an inch. 

The main story with the front will be much colder lows in the low to 
middle 30s by early Saturday. Right now, cloud cover from the 
departing shortwave, and a well-mixed boundary layer from northerly 
winds, may prevent a widespread freeze. However, our northern 
counties from the Triad into the northern Coastal Plain may have a 
good 3-4 hours of below freezing temperatures. Given that, and in 
coordination with neighboring WFOs, decided to issue a Freeze Watch 
for our northern tier for early Saturday. Later forecast shifts may 
adjust the watch as needed.


KEY MESSAGE 2... The chilliest air of the season will arrive and 
support the first widespread frost/freeze risk this weekend, 
followed by continued below average temperatures (including 
additional frost/freezes) and dry conditions that will persist 
through most of next week.

Broad mid/upper troughing over the eastern US on Saturday, 
associated with a mid/upper cyclone over southeastern Canada and 
northern New England, will migrate east into the western Atlantic 
through early next week. Meanwhile, high-amplitude ridging will 
slowly shift east from the Plains into the MS Valley. At the 
surface, high pressure from Central Canada will drop south into the 
Midwest this weekend, then into the OH Valley and central/southern 
Appalachians early next week.

Dry and very chilly conditions will result across central NC during 
this period. We will still be in a CAA regime on Saturday, with NW 
winds gusting to 15-20 mph at times, before the MSLP gradient starts 
to relax as the high gets closer, resulting in calmer winds and 
better radiational cooling conditions on Sunday and Monday mornings. 
There may still be light stirring from a continued gradient on 
Sunday morning, while Monday morning looks calmer, but low-level 
thicknesses start to rise by that point. Regardless which morning is 
colder, the first sub-freezing temperatures of the season are 
expected across much of central NC both days, with a hard freeze 
even possible over outlying parts of the Piedmont. The urban 
Triangle and far SE may be the only areas that have lows at or just 
above freezing. Thus the growing season is likely to be ended this 
weekend. For reference, the last day GSO reached at or below 
freezing was March 18, while it was April 9 at RDU and March 29 at 
FAY. Highs this weekend will also be chilly, only reaching the lower 
to mid 50s on Saturday and mid to upper 50s on Sunday. These would 
be the coolest highs across the area since March. 

Fire weather concerns can't be totally ruled out on Saturday given 
RH values dropping to 30-35% and possibly even lower given NW 
downsloping flow. Momentum transfer on forecast model soundings also 
indicates wind gusts in the 15-20 kt range. But the marginal winds 
combined with the cool temperatures will limit potential for 
increased fire danger.

The Canadian High will remain over the Eastern US from Monday 
through Thursday, with only slow weakening/modification expected. So 
widespread frost/freeze conditions are likely to continue each 
morning through Thursday, and near-normal highs in the lower-to-mid-
60s won't return until Wednesday/Thursday.
